source.title: Tree SAE: Learning Hierarchical Feature Structures in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: T. M. Cao; Hoang X. Nhat; Raed Alharbi; Phi Le Nguyen; My T. Thai

page_placements.theme: SAE architectures that build in a hierarchy

record.tranche_reason: The study measures SAE splitting, absorption, and hierarchical-pair quality, and argues that activation coverage alone is insufficient to establish a meaningful parent-child relationship. Its proposed definition and results refine how hierarchical SAE features should be identified.
record.gate_note: The study trains and evaluates SAEs on GPT2-small layer 5 activations, and reports splitting, absorption, hierarchy, geometry, and child-diversity results. Reported figure values that are not stated numerically in the text are recorded as figure only. Training hyperparameters and MCS setup comparisons used to select procedures are not separate result rows.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a method paper proposing Tree SAE. Two of its results still bear on the claim independently of its own method. First, it reports that Matryoshka SAEs reduce, and MP-SAEs worsen, splitting and absorption relative to Top-k on GPT2-small (V6). Second, it shows with case studies that activation-coverage (MCS) parent–child families in Top-k, Matryoshka and Tree SAEs include semantically unrelated pairs, which qualifies V3. Most recorded rows are Tree SAE's own performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Authors conclude that activation coverage alone yields semantically incoherent parent–child pairs, and propose adding a reconstruction condition. They report that Tree SAE learns substantially more coherent pairs while staying competitive with Matryoshka on splitting, absorption, composition, reconstruction and interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and trains a tree-structured SAE with gated child activations, multi-level reconstruction loss, and dynamic reallocation. It also evaluates Matryoshka, Matching Pursuit, and Top-k SAEs; it is not a direct reproduction of the original dictionary-size splitting analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The hierarchy metric depends on the MCS setup: the authors report non-scaling-binary as best and scaling-correlation as worst. Results are also reported across L0 levels, SAE layer counts, and dictionary sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Tree SAE, which imposes a parent–child tree by architecture, yields more probe-coherent parent–child pairs. It also gives low child co-occurrence (0.010–0.028) and child encoder directions mostly pointing toward child activation clusters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicitly hierarchy-constrained SAE architectures produce more coherent parent–child feature families than independent-feature SAEs.

record.problems: The principal splitting and absorption comparisons are presented in figures without numeric values in the text. The central model evaluation is GPT2-small at layer 5. The child-subspace geometry analysis is qualitative and includes an acknowledged exception. The study's hierarchy metric depends on a probe-based criterion and its selected MCS procedure.

untested.parts: All of it. No single method's splitting is described as changing with dictionary size; Figure 8 values are not stated in the text. No feature is tracked across sizes.
All of it. Only GPT2-small layer 5 is evaluated; Gemma-2-2b is mentioned only for hyperparameters.
Whether absorption persists across size or sparsity for standard SAEs. Top-k absorption values are figure-only, and no Top-k scaling is reported.
Whether splitting says little about the model's own units. Synthetic correlated or hierarchical inputs as the cause are not tested.

missing.what: Hierarchy metric (share of MCS-found pairs meeting both coverage and reconstruction conditions) for Top-k, Matryoshka and MP-SAE
Case studies of spurious activation-coverage children: PCA feature 3098 (Tree), feature 1343 child 15275 (Tree), Matryoshka feature 1605, TopK feature 451
Top-k: probe correlation rising with activation-coverage rank over top-20 children of 100 parents
Splitting/absorption values at 6k, 24k and 49k for Matryoshka (size trend)
Top-k absorption and splitting levels across L0 32–80

record.verdict_notes: Most splitting and absorption evidence is figure-only. The record's V4 'challenges' label is dropped: architecture changes do not bear on V4's size/sparsity claim, and Tree SAE rows are own-method comparisons. Code released; preprint.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures splitting pathology across SAE methods and dictionary sizes, but does not track a particular small-dictionary feature into larger-dictionary features or directly test whether those features partition the same inputs and lie near the original feature direction.
The main reported evaluation is GPT2-small at layer 5; there is no reported cross-model or open-SAE-release test of the claim.
The study evaluates learned parent-child relationships and child-subspace geometry, but does not establish that these structures mirror a complete hierarchy of concepts in the language model.
The study measures benchmark feature absorption and reports scaling comparisons, but does not directly track a particular parent latent's firing on the cases where a child takes over.
It does not test whether larger-SAE latents decompose into combinations of smaller-SAE latents or whether larger SAEs add novel latents.

The study compares splitting metrics across SAE methods and reports results for its Tree SAE and Matryoshka SAE, but does not establish that splitting is an artifact rather than a model property, nor test correlated or hierarchical synthetic inputs as the cause.

relation.reason: The case studies and baseline comparisons bear on V3 and V6 independently of the Tree SAE method.

tranche.reason: The paper argues activation coverage alone gives incoherent parent-child pairs, which restates V3. It also gives baseline Matryoshka and MP-SAE comparisons that bear on V6.

source_check.notes: All benchmark values are figure-only (Figs 3-5, 8); only GPT2-small layer 5 tested, with Matryoshka/Top-k/MP-SAE at 24k features only. MP-SAE L0 is adaptive and not stated. Appendix E text and the Fig 17/18 captions swap figure numbers and disagree on which Matryoshka child (16758 vs 23918) is unrelated. The MCS-variant comparison used Tree SAEs only. The Tree SAE hierarchy is imposed by architecture.

statements.problem: The parts about this study (unrelated political-token child under a time feature) match Section 2.2 and Fig 1. The ESM and WordNet parts are about other studies.

statements.correction: Four MCS variants (binary or not, scaled or not) were compared on Tree SAEs only, across all L0 levels (Fig 20). Non-scaling-binary was best and scaling-correlation worst, and non-scaling-binary was then used for all MCS runs. Hierarchy-metric results across L0 (Fig 4) and dictionary size (Fig 5, Tree vs Matryoshka only) are figure-only.
statements.problem: The MCS-setup comparison (non-scaling-binary best, scaling-correlation worst) was run on Tree SAEs only (Appendix G, Fig 20), not across dictionary sizes. The statement names no SAE, so it reads as general.

statements.correction: 2605.07922 r2, r8: GPT2-small layer 5, 24576 features, L0 32-80. Matryoshka (2- and 4-layer) and Tree SAEs reach strong splitting and absorption performance vs Top-k (not BatchTopK) at every L0. Figure-only (Fig 3), no numeric rates.
statements.problem: Cites this study's r2 and r8, but the text and conditions cover only Gemma-2-2B/Llama-3-8B and Matryoshka vs BatchTopK. r2/r8 are GPT2-small vs Top-k with no numbers.
